paper_title: PixelOne: From Options to Pixels in a Single Forward for GUI Grounding

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: GUI grounding requires precise clicks at low latency. Recent models such as GUI-Decisions and GUI-Swift predict coordinates in one forward pass using fixed global bins with local refinement. However, screenshot downsampling removes detail needed to locate small controls, while fixed bins cover larger pixel ranges at higher resolutions. We introduce PixelOne, which transfers spatial knowledge from a search teacher to a student that predicts clicks directly from screenshots at native resolution. The teacher uses VideoJEV's text-option scorer to select rows and columns and progressively zoom into candidate regions. The student inherits the teacher's parameters and matches its distributions over explored regions through spatial distillation alongside box supervision. At inference, the same decision head selects a visual token, and a lightweight pixel head predicts the click within it, all in one forward pass. A click-aligned loss encourages pixels inside the target box to score above those outside. Across four benchmarks, PixelOne-Pro-35B-A3B achieves 83.8% mean accuracy, the highest among the evaluated single-forward grounders, with a mean latency of 0.43 s per target.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: A GUI agent translates instructions, such as open the alignment menu, into corresponding click locations on screenshot [1, 3, 13, 22, 25, 28, 36, 39, 40, 42, 43]. This requires accurate visual grounding, particularly in high-resolution interfaces where small interactive targets are often surrounded by visually similar controls, making the preservation of fine-grained spatial details essential [14, 18, 45]. Consequently, practical GUI agent is required to localize target elements accurately with low latency [2]. Spatial readouts predict clicks directly from scores over image regions or target masks [32, 34]. By contrast, fixed-slot methods such as GUI-Decisions and GUI-Swift predict distributions over global coordinate bins at predefined token positions and refine the coordinates using neighboring-bin probabilities [8, 31]. Both approaches avoid autoregressive coordinate generation and ground targets in single forward pass. However, these models downsample high-resolution screenshots, removing details needed to locate small controls, while their global bins cover large pixel ranges at higher resolutions. These limitations motivate direct readout 1 Figure 1 PixelOne-Pro on the accuracylatency frontier. The main plot compares mean accuracy and latency across four benchmarks. The ScreenSpot Pro and OSWorld-G insets each compare both Pro models with the four highest-scoring external GUI-specialized baselines. The leaderboard bars use truncated linear accuracy scale from 50% to 80%. Full results and timing details appear in Table 1 and Section S4.4. that preserves image detail and predicts clicks at pixel granularity. Native decision models provide starting point through an interface for scoring candidate options [7, 9, 12, 41, 47]. VideoJEV uses this interface to select textual answers and temporal intervals [48]. Extending it to pixel localization requires spatial candidates tied to screenshot regions and way to resolve click within the selected region. We introduce PixelOne, teacher-student framework for accurate GUI grounding from full-resolution screenshots in single forward pass. During training, search teacher learns to localize targets by choosing rows and columns from textual spatial options. It progressively narrows the target location across full-image and zoomed views using box supervision (Figure 2). The student inherits the teachers network and query/key decision head. The teacher also provides distributions over the regions explored during search, which complement the students box supervision. This transfer is possible because the same head scores both forms of spatial evidence (Figure 3): textual options in the teacher and visual tokens in the student. At inference, the student applies the shared decision head to visual tokens from the full-resolution screenshot and selects the token most relevant to the instruction. PixelOne determines the precise click within that region as the selected token localizes the target only to an area. pixel head predicts this point using features from the same forward pass. Assigning high probability to pixels inside the target does not guarantee the top-ranked pixel is valid click. We therefore introduce click-aligned objective that encourages valid pixels to score higher than pixels outside the target. PixelOne returns click location with one visual encoding and one pass through the language model, without iterative search or autoregressive coordinate generation. We train PixelOne in two settings: the standard version updates language LoRA and both readout heads, whereas PixelOne-Pro updates the entire model. Across four benchmarks, PixelOne-Pro-35B-A3B achieves 83.8% mean accuracy at an average latency of 0.43 per click, ranking first among the evaluated singleforward grounders. Pro-4B reaches 80.6% at 0.32 s, and both models lie on the accuracylatency frontier (Table 1 and Figure 1). Ablations across both model scales demonstrate the benefits of spatial distillation and the click-aligned objective (Tables 2, 4 and 5). 2 Figure 2 From spatial search to single-forward grounding. (a) The teacher scores row and column choices with VideoJEVs native head. (b) The teacher refines candidate regions through zoomed search. (c) The student inherits the teachers shared parameters and learns from its spatial distributions to predict click with one visual encoding and one model forward. Our contributions are: Native pixel-decision interface. We adapt VideoJEVs head to visual tokens and resolve clicks with lightweight pixel head trained with click-aligned objective. Search-to-pixel learning. We share decision parameters across textual search options and visual tokens, transferring both the teachers weights and its spatial distributions to the student. Accurate and efficient grounding. PixelOne grounds full-resolution screenshots in one forward pass at 4B and 35B-A3B, with both Pro variants on the evaluated accuracylatency frontier.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Coordinate generation and direct readout. Autoregressive grounders represent coordinates and action fields as text [6, 24, 30, 38]. This flexible interface requires sequential decoding, whereas direct readouts predict locations in single forward pass. GUI-Actor and V2P score visual patches with dedicated head, while GUI-AIMA supervises attention within the backbone [5, 34, 46]. Seg2Click instead predicts action masks at the pixel level [32]. Fixed-slot methods such as GUI-Decisions and GUI-Swift take another route, reading coordinates from predefined positions through the vocabulary head [8, 31]. Although these methods avoid sequential decoding, precise grounding still depends on sufficient image detail and reliably converting spatial scores into clicks. Spatial detail and inference cost. Higher-resolution screenshots preserve the detail needed to locate small targets but increase inference cost [10]. GUI-Decisions and GUI-Swift limit the number of visual tokens and therefore downsample large screenshots [8, 31]. They also predict coordinates using fixed global bins with refinement from neighboring-bin probabilities; as resolution increases, each bin covers larger pixel range. Other methods recover local detail through additional computation. Zoomed search processes cropped regions, while Re-Prefill uses attention to guide second prefill stage [18, 19]. InnerZoom avoids another round of image encoding by refining regional evidence within the decoder layers, although it still generates coordinates autoregressively [21]. An alternative is to move spatial refinement into training, allowing the model to learn from detailed local views without repeating the process at inference time. Transferring search knowledge to direct prediction. Methods that transfer knowledge from refined views differ in what they teach the student. Region-to-Image Distillation turns zoomed regions into question 3 Figure 3 One decision head, two kinds of options. (a) The teacher uses the native decision head to score text options. (b) PixelOne reuses this head to select visual token and adds pixel head to locate the click within it. and answer pairs for models that process the full image [33]. Native decision models provide different signal by assigning probabilities to set of options [9, 12, 23, 47]. These options may represent actions from an accessibility tree, as in Jev-Mobile, or regions proposed by segmenter, as in AffordJEV [17, 44]. VideoJEV further shows that the same scoring interface can evaluate textual answers and temporal intervals from video evidence [48]. PixelOne uses this interface for spatial search and transfers both the learned parameters and the resulting distributions over image regions to direct predictor. The student then scores visual tokens and predicts precise click from the full-resolution screenshot in one forward pass.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: PixelOne takes screenshot and an instruction as input and predicts click location ˆp. The prediction is considered correct if ˆp lies inside the target box B. Our goal is to predict this point directly from the full screenshot while learning from the finer spatial decisions made during search. To this end, we first train teacher to locate the target through sequence of row and column choices (Figure 2). We then transfer its knowledge to student that operates without search. The student uses the teachers decision head to select visual token and lightweight pixel head to determine the click within that token (Figure 3). It inherits the teachers parameters and learns from both the teachers spatial distributions and the target box. At inference time, the student receives only (I, u) and predicts the click with one visual encoding and one pass through the model.

The scale α = 10 and bias remain fixed during teacher training. Softmax is applied separately to the row, column, and visibility option sets. The three-round search (T3) begins with 4 4 grid over the full screenshot. The score of each cell is the product of its row and column probabilities. The teacher retains the two cells with the highest scores. In each of the next two rounds, the teacher places an 88 grid over crop corresponding to each retained cell. For every crop, it receives both the enlarged crop and full-image overview that marks the crop location. It also answers visibility question that asks whether the target is present in the crop. child score is obtained by multiplying its row and column probabilities by the visibility probability of the crop and the score of its parent. The teacher then retains the two highest-scoring children across both crops. After the third round, it returns the center of the best final cell as ˆpT . The two crop states in each refinement round are processed as batch, resulting in three language-model calls and five visual-encoder calls per target (Figure 2). We first train the teacher on global and local states derived from target boxes. We then run the partially trained teacher on subset of the training examples and collect the states visited during search. For each visited crop, the center of the target box defines the row and column labels whenever it falls inside the crop. The visibility label is positive when the crop fully contains the target box and negative when the crop does not overlap it. For partial overlaps, we omit the visibility loss while retaining any valid row and column supervision. Training then continues on mixture of visited states and states derived from target boxes [29]. Finally, we freeze the teacher and cache its search traces (Section S2.2). The teachers weights initialize the student, while the cached distributions provide spatial supervision.

sections.title: 4.5 Region Selection and Pixel Precision
sections.content: We analyze the single-winner students in Table 3, pooling evaluation targets. Target-token coverage measures how often the selected token contains valid click, while conditional pixel accuracy measures click accuracy within this subset. Initialization strengthens region selection. Teacher initialization improves target-token coverage at both scales in Figure 5a. The error breakdown in Section S6.4 shows that most of the gain comes from fewer selections far from the target, indicating stronger global localization. Spatial KD strengthens pixel precision. Spatial KD improves conditional pixel accuracy at both scales while maintaining similar targettoken coverage. On ScreenSpot Pro at 35B-A3B, within-token pixel errors fall from 251 to 185, while the number of targets with correct token selection changes only from 1,070 to 1,075. The category results in Table S10 show gains for both text and icon targets. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: PixelOne transfers search teachers parameters and spatial distributions to student that predicts clicks directly from the full screenshot in single forward pass. Its shared decision head selects visual token, while lightweight pixel head trained with click-aligned objective locates the click within that token. Experiments across four benchmarks validate the contributions of spatial distillation and click-aligned pixel learning. PixelOne-Pro-35B-A3B achieves 83.8% mean accuracy with mean latency of 0.43 per target, while both the 4B and 35B-A3B configurations lie on the accuracylatency frontier of the evaluated systems. More broadly, PixelOne offers design principle for efficient GUI grounding: move spatial exploration into training and align supervision with the executed click, enabling richer spatial learning without performing search at inference time.
